===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS spaced-repetition flashcard app called "Recall". Native Apple stack ONLY: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, Swift Charts for stats. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network of any kind — the app must work in airplane mode forever, all data on-device. Follow the ios-app-factory-rules. Runnable in the iOS Simulator via Xcode; provide clear run instructions.

HARD RULE ON GAPS: Anything that would need infrastructure this project cannot provide (cloud sync, shared/community decks, a deck marketplace) must NOT be faked or stubbed. Record each honestly as a gap with a short note on what building it for real would take. Do not add placeholder UI that pretends these work.

CORE FEATURES (favor complete over broad):
1. Decks & cards: create/edit/archive decks; cards have a front, back, and optional note. Card editing must be fast and keyboard-friendly.
2. Spaced-repetition scheduling: implement the SM-2 algorithm (ease factor, interval, repetition count) with Again/Hard/Good/Easy grading. THIS IS THE HEART OF THE APP. Implement it as its own standalone, pure, tested module — provably right, not plausibly right. Unit tests MUST cover: first reviews, lapses resetting the interval, ease-factor floors, and day-boundary handling in the device's local time zone (a "day" is a calendar day).
3. Review session: shows due cards for a chosen deck (or all decks); front → tap to reveal → grade. Session summary at end (cards reviewed, again-rate, time spent). Must handle interruption gracefully — quitting mid-session loses nothing.
4. Stats: per-deck and overall — due-forecast bar chart for next 30 days, daily review-count history, and retention rate (% graded Good/Easy). Handle empty and sparse data gracefully.
5. Deck import/export: export any deck to CSV; import cards from a two-column CSV (front, back) with a preview step and per-row error reporting — never silently drop a row.
6. Review reminders: one optional LOCAL notification per day ("You have N cards due") at a user-chosen time; respect permission denial gracefully. No push, no server.

PRIORITIES (in order): (1) SM-2 module correctness above all — proven via its tests; (2) review-flow speed; (3) honest empty states. Include a "demo data" toggle in Settings that seeds two decks with a realistic review history so stats screens are never empty on first look.

**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Recall is for people who treat review as a recurring routine, not a one-off study burst: language learners, exam candidates, and professionals who memorize recurring material, and who actually review in short windows (while commuting, before bed, or in airports). The value is that Recall removes scheduling uncertainty from the loop. It tells you exactly which cards are due for today on the device, updates the moment you answer, and never asks you to trust a server, an account, or a sync status you can’t see.

The paid value has to be about speed, certainty, and time saved after the first week, not cosmetic skinning. Free can deliver the full foundation: offline data model in SwiftData, SM-2 review, immediate persistence, CSV import/export, reminders, and core charts. Pro should be a functional upgrade that helps serious users study faster and with better calibration: stronger analytics (deck-level and historical trend interpretation, missed-card diagnostics, weekly “what to trim” recommendations), review cadence hardening (exam mode presets, configurable interruption-safe session chunking), and a “review integrity pack” for power users (scheduled review plan previews, deeper retention confidence stats, and CSV validation diagnostics for big imports). The premium line is that it converts card volume and noisy study sessions into predictable, reviewable outcomes instead of feeling like a growing pile.

The product promise in use is: pick deck scope, Reveal/grade due cards with Again/Hard/Good/Easy, save immediately, and stop at any interruption point without losing anything already graded. The critical habit loop is short and repeatable; under three minutes to start, one card-at-a-time reveal-to-grade flow, then a short, honest summary. A good reminder implementation closes the loop by making the app feel reliable: one local daily notification with real permission state and a truthful “enable in Settings” path when denied.

The competitive wedge is not raw flashcard functionality. Anki, Quizlet, and similar tools are useful but imply heavier setup, account flows, or cloud assumptions and less predictability around local, timezone-sensitive due state. Recall should position itself around “provable local trust”: pure SM-2 core, on-device-only persistence, and no fake outcomes. The differentiator is not more features; it is dependable review correctness under real-world conditions like plane mode, force quits, timezone travel, and interrupted sessions.

The local-first behavior is explicit: all data, scheduling state, reminders, and stats are persisted locally, and every UI state is derivable from local store state. There is one shared due-calculation pathway fed by the same scheduling model and calendar-day semantics everywhere it appears (deck badge counts, review scope screens, reminders, charts), so no screen can lie differently about what is due. App startup must handle empty and sparse datasets with designed “you’re all set” empties, not placeholders or fake progress.

Cloud-ready extension should be additive, not a rewrite: keep the pure scheduling engine, repository boundaries, and models cleanly separated so later phases can add an optional sync adapter (iCloud or another provider) without changing the SM-2 or persistence contracts. Future sync can be opt-in and conflict-aware, but never required for v1. If sync is added later, it should still obey the same local-first invariant: work uninterrupted when offline, resolve conflicts explicitly, and never block review on network availability.

Growth should come from niche trust and portability, not broad social features. The strongest mechanism is community-to-study-circle reuse of deck CSVs that already fits the offline model: students exchange two-column decks through Notes, AirDrop, and Files, then get immediate utility through the same deterministic schedule. That creates a credible network effect in specific communities (language classrooms, exam prep cohorts, residency programs) without fake social features or account scaffolding. The keep factor is mostly behavioral trust: users stay if they believe the next-review date is right every time they return.

The decision that must survive every implementation step is this: if a review is graded, it must be safely persisted and the queue logic must remain correct to the calendar-day model under interruption, clock changes, and DST shifts. If that single invariant slips, all other differentiation collapses.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

Target user and use case: the same self-directed learner locked in earlier — language learners, board/certification candidates, and professionals maintaining recurring domain knowledge — but I want to be blunt about the paid user specifically: it's the subset of that population who already has more than a casual amount of material to memorize (a full MCAT deck, a language vocabulary that grows past a few hundred cards, a professional certification with multiple subject decks). Casual users with one deck of 50 cards never need to pay, and that's fine — they're the free funnel, not the target.

Free tier: unlimited cards inside up to two active (non-archived, non-demo) decks, full and uncompromised SM-2 scheduling with zero correctness gating ever, the complete review flow, and one basic stat — today's due count and a simple streak. That's a genuinely usable, complete app for a light user, not a crippled demo. Paid tier (subscription, e.g. monthly/annual, priced like a habit app not a suite): unlimited decks, the full Stats screen (30-day forecast, daily history, retention rate — all three, not a teaser chart), CSV import (bulk deck creation from an existing pile of notes), and the daily reminder notification. That split is the deliberate decision: the free tier proves the algorithm works and feels great in short sessions; the paid tier is for people whose study load has outgrown "a couple of decks" and who want to see their retention trend and bulk-import an existing collection instead of typing it by hand. This is functional gating, not a cosmetic skin — someone with 6 decks and 2,000 cards cannot use this app without paying, and that's the honest value proposition. Deck export to CSV stays free always, deliberately, because it's the user's own data and gating an export path on data you already own is the kind of trust violation that kills an offline-trust app's whole premise.

Core loop doesn't change from what's already locked: pick a deck or all decks, see only what's actually due today, tap-reveal-grade, immediate persist, summary. What I'd add from the QA seat is the exact test that proves the subscription doesn't compromise that loop: a user who never subscribes and never will must get 100% correct SM-2 behavior forever on their two free decks — there is no version of this app where paying changes how a card is scheduled, only how much you can store and how much insight you can see. If that boundary blurs even slightly, the "trust the algorithm" promise from initial_discussion collapses.

Competitive wedge: Anki is free but demands the user assemble their own trust in an aging, unpolished sync-heavy tool; Quizlet is polished but account/cloud-dependent and increasingly ad/subscription-cluttered around content, not scheduling; Brainscape doesn't hold to strict SM-2 or interruption-safety guarantees at all (per the earlier research phase, that's an assumption, not a sourced fact, but it's the right positioning target). Recall's wedge is narrow and defensible: a native, fast, offline-forever app whose entire pitch is "the schedule is never wrong and never depends on a server," proven by a public, testable algorithm module rather than asserted. That's a hard thing for a bigger, feature-sprawled competitor to credibly claim, because they're all carrying sync/account complexity that Recall explicitly refuses.

Growth angle, and I want to be concrete instead of hand-wavy: there's no marketplace, no sharing feature to build, and I'm not proposing one. But the CSV export we're already required to build is a de facto shareable artifact — a plain two-column file a user can already AirDrop, text, or post to a study subreddit or Discord using the OS share sheet we already need for export. That's not a feature we invent, it's a side effect of feature 5 that becomes the growth mechanic: "made a great vocab deck? Send the CSV to a friend." Positioned as onboarding, the CSV importer doubles as a migration wedge — "already have cards in Anki, Quizlet, or a spreadsheet? Import them in under a minute" — using a feature we're building anyway, not a marketing feature we'd need to invent. Niche growth channel: exam-prep and language-learning communities that already trade flashcard files informally are the natural first audience, reached by ordinary App Store discovery and word of mouth, not by any in-app viral mechanic that doesn't exist here.

Local-first behavior is non-negotiable and already locked from earlier phases: everything — free and paid — runs from on-device SwiftData with zero network calls for actual app function. The one and only place network touches this app is the App Store purchase transaction itself, which is inherent to StoreKit and not a violation of "airplane mode forever" — a user can buy the subscription once with connectivity and then use every paid feature offline permanently afterward, verified via on-device `Transaction.currentEntitlements`, no server round-trip on each launch. Cloud-ready path forward, explicitly not built now: keep the SwiftData schema CloudKit-shaped — stable UUIDs as primary identity, no force-unwrapped relationships, no compound keys that don't survive CKRecord translation — so that a future version could offer opt-in iCloud sync as a first-party (not custom-backend) extension without a data-model rewrite. That stays a documented future path with zero UI implying it exists today, consistent with the hard rule on gaps.

Biggest risk I'd flag against my own proposal: subscription pricing on an app whose most credible competitor (Anki) is free could suppress conversion if the paid tier is perceived as thin. My answer to that risk is to make the cap itself the argument — two decks is enough to try it seriously but not enough to run, say, a full MCAT or a growing language vocabulary, so the paywall is hit exactly when the user has proven to themselves the algorithm works and now has real inventory to manage. The detail I most want preserved into the next phase: free-tier SM-2 correctness and the core review loop are permanently ungated, the deck cap and full Stats/CSV-import/reminders are the paid boundary, and expiry degrades access without ever deleting user data.

# First-Party Apple Frameworks Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / Swift 5.9+)

Build capable iPhone apps with **zero third-party dependencies**. For each framework: when to reach for it, the entry-point type, and a compilable, idiomatic snippet or the gotcha that bites people. All examples target **iOS 17 minimum** unless a call-out says otherwise; Swift Concurrency (`async`/`await`) is preferred over completion handlers everywhere Apple offers it.

## General rules

- **Prefer these over SPM packages.** RevenueCat, Firebase Analytics, Lottie, Alamofire, etc. all have first-party equivalents good enough for most apps. Fewer deps = smaller binary, faster builds, no supply-chain risk, no privacy-manifest surprises.
- **Every framework that touches user data needs an `Info.plist` usage-description string** (or an entitlement). Missing it is a runtime crash the moment the API is used — not a compile error. The specific keys are listed per section.
- **Import the framework and its SwiftUI companion when one exists** (e.g. `import MapKit` gives you `Map`; `import StoreKit` gives you `SubscriptionStoreView`/`StoreView`).
- **Do capability checks before hardware-dependent APIs** (`CHHapticEngine.capabilitiesForHardware().supportsHaptics`, `HKHealthStore.isHealthDataAvailable()`, `GKLocalPlayer.local.isAuthenticated`). Simulators and older/cheaper devices lie.
- **Never block the main actor.** Long queries, audio-graph setup, and StoreKit calls belong in `Task {}` or `async` functions.
- **Verify APIs against the deployment target.** Several SwiftUI conveniences (e.g. `GameCenterView`, Control widgets) shipped *after* iOS 17. Availability call-outs below flag these.

func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {

**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Recall is for people who treat review as a recurring routine, not a one-off study burst: language learners, exam candidates, and professionals who memorize recurring material, and who actually review in short windows (while commuting, before bed, or in airports). The value is that Recall removes scheduling uncertainty from the loop. It tells you exactly which cards are due for today on the device, updates the moment you answer, and never asks you to trust a server, an account, or a sync status you can’t see.

The paid value has to be about speed, certainty, and time saved after the first week, not cosmetic skinning. Free can deliver the full foundation: offline data model in SwiftData, SM-2 review, immediate persistence, CSV import/export, reminders, and core charts. Pro should be a functional upgrade that helps serious users study faster and with better calibration: stronger analytics (deck-level and historical trend interpretation, missed-card diagnostics, weekly “what to trim” recommendations), review cadence hardening (exam mode presets, configurable interruption-safe session chunking), and a “review integrity pack” for power users (scheduled review plan previews, deeper retention confidence stats, and CSV validation diagnostics for big imports). The premium line is that it converts card volume and noisy study sessions into predictable, reviewable outcomes instead of feeling like a growing pile.

The product promise in use is: pick deck scope, Reveal/grade due cards with Again/Hard/Good/Easy, save immediately, and stop at any interruption point without losing anything already graded. The critical habit loop is short and repeatable; under three minutes to start, one card-at-a-time reveal-to-grade flow, then a short, honest summary. A good reminder implementation closes the loop by making the app feel reliable: one local daily notification with real permission state and a truthful “enable in Settings” path when denied.

The competitive wedge is not raw flashcard functionality. Anki, Quizlet, and similar tools are useful but imply heavier setup, account flows, or cloud assumptions and less predictability around local, timezone-sensitive due state. Recall should position itself around “provable local trust”: pure SM-2 core, on-device-only persistence, and no fake outcomes. The differentiator is not more features; it is dependable review correctness under real-world conditions like plane mode, force quits, timezone travel, and interrupted sessions.

The local-first behavior is explicit: all data, scheduling state, reminders, and stats are persisted locally, and every UI state is derivable from local store state. There is one shared due-calculation pathway fed by the same scheduling model and calendar-day semantics everywhere it appears (deck badge counts, review scope screens, reminders, charts), so no screen can lie differently about what is due. App startup must handle empty and sparse datasets with designed “you’re all set” empties, not placeholders or fake progress.

Cloud-ready extension should be additive, not a rewrite: keep the pure scheduling engine, repository boundaries, and models cleanly separated so later phases can add an optional sync adapter (iCloud or another provider) without changing the SM-2 or persistence contracts. Future sync can be opt-in and conflict-aware, but never required for v1. If sync is added later, it should still obey the same local-first invariant: work uninterrupted when offline, resolve conflicts explicitly, and never block review on network availability.

Growth should come from niche trust and portability, not broad social features. The strongest mechanism is community-to-study-circle reuse of deck CSVs that already fits the offline model: students exchange two-column decks through Notes, AirDrop, and Files, then get immediate utility through the same deterministic schedule. That creates a credible network effect in specific communities (language classrooms, exam prep cohorts, residency programs) without fake social features or account scaffolding. The keep factor is mostly behavioral trust: users stay if they believe the next-review date is right every time they return.

The decision that must survive every implementation step is this: if a review is graded, it must be safely persisted and the queue logic must remain correct to the calendar-day model under interruption, clock changes, and DST shifts. Build capable iPhone apps with **zero third-party dependencies**. For each framework: when to reach for it, the entry-point type, and a compilable, idiomatic snippet or the gotcha that bites people. All examples target **iOS 17 minimum** unless a call-out says otherwise; Swift Concurrency (`async`/`await`) is preferred over completion handlers everywhere Apple offers it.

## General rules

- **Every framework that touches user data needs an `Info.plist` usage-description string** (or an entitlement). Missing it is a runtime crash the moment the API is used — not a compile error. The specific keys are listed per section.
- **Import the framework and its SwiftUI companion when one exists** (e.g. `import MapKit` gives you `Map`; `import StoreKit` gives you `SubscriptionStoreView`/`StoreView`).

- **Never block the main actor.** Long queries, audio-graph setup, and StoreKit calls belong in `Task {}` or `async` functions.

## StoreKit 2 — In-App Purchase & Subscriptions

**Use it when:** you sell anything — consumables, non-consumables, or auto-renewable subscriptions. Replaces callback-based StoreKit 1 entirely.

**Start from:** `Product` (fetch + purchase) and `Transaction` (entitlements + history). No server strictly required — signatures are verified on-device via `VerificationResult`.

### The three things you must do

1. **Load products by ID** (IDs come from App Store Connect):

```swift
import StoreKit

let productIDs = ["com.app.pro.monthly", "com.app.pro.yearly", "com.app.coins.100"]
let products = try await Product.products(for: productIDs)   // async throws
```

2. **Purchase, then verify and finish the transaction:**

```swift
func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {
    let result = try await product.purchase()
    switch result {
    case .success(let verification):
        let transaction = try checkVerified(verification)
        await transaction.finish()          // REQUIRED — unfinished txns replay forever
        return transaction
    case .userCancelled, .pending:
        return nil
    @unknown default:
        return nil
    }
}

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant
    case .verified(let safe):       return safe
    }
}
```

3. **Listen for `Transaction.updates` from app launch** — the single most-missed requirement. It catches renewals, Ask-to-Buy approvals, refunds, and purchases made on other devices.

```swift
// Start this in your App init / a top-level task and keep it alive for the app's lifetime.
func observeTransactions() -> Task<Void, Never> {
    Task.detached {
        for await update in Transaction.updates {
            guard case .verified(let transaction) = update else { continue }
            await grantEntitlement(for: transaction)   // your unlock logic
            await transaction.finish()
        }
    }
}
```

Use `Transaction.currentEntitlements` (an async sequence). **iOS 18.4+ note:** the per-product `Transaction.currentEntitlement(for:)` is deprecated in favor of `Transaction.currentEntitlements(for:)`, because a user can hold multiple entitling transactions (e.g. own it *and* have Family Sharing access).

```swift
func hasActiveSubscription() async -> Bool {
    for await result in Transaction.currentEntitlements {
        guard case .verified(let transaction) = result else { continue }
        if transaction.productType == .autoRenewable && transaction.revocationDate == nil {
